teaser.text: METRO is a Canadian food and pharmacy retailer and distributor, with most of its stores in Québec and Ontario. To understand its business, follow a dollar from the shopper or store operator to METRO, and then through the costs of getting products onto the shelf.

dividend.title: METRO dividend
dividend.meta_description: METRO's dividend, cash coverage, payout choices, outlook and yield, in plain English.
dividend.opening: METRO currently pays CAD 0.4075 per share each quarter. METRO generated C$811.5 million of free cash flow and C$797.7 million of real free cash flow in fiscal 2025, but shareholder payouts exceeded free cash flow in each year shown.
dividend.closing: The full memo also examines METRO's business, its rivals, its management, and its risks.

blocks.heading: How much does METRO pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: Dividends rise more slowly than their recent history. The base case moves from CAD 1.68 per share to CAD 1.84. The bear case holds the current annualized rate at CAD 1.63, while the bull case reaches CAD 2.01. The current quarterly dividend is CAD 0.4075 and was unchanged from the prior quarter. Operating cash was below the prior-year level during the first 40 weeks. The base path is supported by METRO’s record of annual increases, but it assumes slower growth than the past five years.

blocks.heading: Is METRO's dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow is the cash left after capital spending, lease payments and interest paid. METRO’s fiscal-2025 free cash flow was C$811.5 million. Its “real free cash flow” was C$797.7 million after stock-based compensation. These are useful owner-focused measures, but they are not standard IFRS measures.

The five-year record shows shareholder payouts above free cash flow in each year. Dividends are recurring payments to all shareholders; buybacks are more discretionary purchases that reduce the number of shares outstanding. When payouts exceed free cash flow, METRO must draw on existing cash, sell assets, issue shares or borrow.

blocks.heading: What is METRO's dividend yield today?

paragraphs.text: METRO trades at 23.1x trailing P/E and 17.8x forward, making earnings recovery central. METRO’s free cash flow is computed from cash from operations minus capital spending, lease payments and interest paid and implies a 4.0% yield. The dividend yield is 1.7%; the 3.9% buyback yield needs context because payouts exceeded free cash flow in each of the five years shown. Net debt rose from C$2,191.0 million in 2021. It reached C$2,888.0 million in 2025 as diluted share count fell each year. Rising sales alone did not establish stronger demand or operating performance.

earnings.title: METRO earnings
earnings.meta_description: METRO's next results are November 18, 2026; guidance is 2%–4% sales growth and 8%–10% adjusted diluted EPS growth.
earnings.opening: METRO's next results are expected on November 18, 2026. METRO's key watch is whether food traffic and margins recover after Laval.
earnings.closing: The full METRO memo also answers questions about METRO's business, its rivals, its management and its risks.

blocks.heading: What has METRO guided for FY2027?

paragraphs.text: METRO’s price can reach C$114.62 by October 2029, hinging on food recovery, pharmacy growth, productivity gains and the valuation multiple. That implies a 23% total return including dividends. Management targets annual sales growth of 2%–4% and adjusted diluted EPS growth of 8%–10%, assuming no material labour or distribution-centre disruption. By the end of FY2027, it expects C$7.5 million in recurring annualized net earnings improvement from network changes. The plan includes 10 Metro-to-Food-Basics conversions.

Management expects recurring annualized net earnings improvement by the end of Fiscal 2027. Annualized means the full-year run rate once the changes are complete, not cash already earned. A separate provincial tax holiday related to Terrebonne’s automated distribution centre supports earnings through approximately Fiscal 2027, but it is temporary and cannot substitute for lasting operating savings.

blocks.heading: Did METRO keep its past earnings promise?

paragraphs.text: Before Q3, METRO guided adjusted earnings per share, or adjusted EPS, of C$1.22–C$1.27. It reported C$1.24, inside that range. Adjusted EPS is profit per share after removing or rearranging items management treats as unusual. It aims to show the ongoing business more clearly, much as a household budget might separate a regular salary from a one-time repair bill.

blocks.heading: What has METRO's revenue and profit trend been over the last eight quarters?

paragraphs.text: Profit fell more sharply than sales. Gross margin declined to 18.8% from 19.8%, while operating income fell to C$330.0 million from C$470.8 million. METRO estimated the strike’s effect at C$90 million before tax and C$66 million after tax. The damage included lost sales and margins, inventory losses, third-party logistics and security costs. METRO did not adjust reported net earnings for the strike.

blocks.heading: What should METRO watchers look for in the next results?

paragraphs.text: The strike lasted nearly six months. Workers ratified a new collective agreement on September 24, with a gradual return to work beginning September 27. METRO said the return would be gradual because its contingency network was less effective than its own network. The important evidence will be the speed of returning traffic, assortment and sales, alongside the lasting distribution costs created by the new agreement.
